blocks.text: The apparent change in the frequency (or pitch) of waves due to the relative motion between the source and observer (listener) is called Doppler Effect.

This effect was first observed by John Doppler while he was observing the frequency of light emitted from a star. In some cases, the frequency of emitted light was found to be slightly different from that emitted from a similar source on the Earth. He found that the change of frequency of light depends upon motion of star relative to Earth.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The effect is named after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler (Christian Andreas Doppler, 1803–1853), not “John Doppler”.

This effect can be observed with sound waves also. For example, when an observer is standing on a railway platform, the pitch of whistle of an engine coming towards the platform appears to become higher to an observer standing on the platform. However, the pitch of whistle of an engine going away from the platform appears to become lower to an observer standing on the platform.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: As a plane accelerates, it builds up a front of air pressure by pushing air in front of it. When it passes the speed of sound, the pressure trails behind like a boat's wake, forming a sonic shockwave.

blocks.alt: Three aircraft with their sound wavefronts. (a) Subsonic speed: the circular wavefronts stay ahead of the nose. (b) At the speed of sound: the wavefronts pile up and overlap at the nose (Overlapping). (c) Supersonic speed: the wavefronts trail behind inside a cone whose edges form the Shockwave. Wavefront labels point to the circles.
blocks.caption: Do You Know? (PDF page 165): an aircraft below, at and above the speed of sound, forming a shockwave (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Panel (a) is printed 'Supersonic speed', but its wavefronts run ahead of the aircraft, which happens below the speed of sound. It is labelled 'Subsonic speed' above.

blocks.title: Example 7.10
blocks.problem:
Two trucks P and Q travelling along a motorway in the same direction. The loading truck P travels at a steady speed of 12 m s⁻¹, the other truck Q, travelling at a steady speed of 20 m s⁻¹, sound its horn to emit a steady note which P's driver estimate, has a frequency of 830 Hz. What frequency does Q's own driver hear?
(Speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
steps:
u_P = 12 m s⁻¹
u_Q = 20 m s⁻¹
v = 340 m s⁻¹
f_P = 830 Hz
f_Q = ?
Speed of Q relative to P = uₛ = u_Q − u_P = 20 − 12 = 8 m s⁻¹

∵ f = (v/(v − uₛ)) f′
∴ f_P = (v/(v − uₛ)) f_Q

blocks.alt: Two trucks facing right: grey truck Q behind, labelled Source (20 m s^-1), and blue truck P ahead, labelled Listener (12 m s^-1).
blocks.caption: Example 7.10 (PDF page 166): truck Q, the source at 20 m s⁻¹, behind truck P, the listener at 12 m s⁻¹ (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.title: Example 7.11
blocks.problem:
A train sounds its horn before it sets off from the station and an observer waiting on the platform estimates its frequency at 1200 Hz. The train then moves off and accelerates steadily. Fifty seconds after departure, the driver sounds the horn again and the platform observer estimates the frequency at 1140 Hz. Calculate the train speed 50 s after departure. How far from the station is the train after 50 s.
(Speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
steps:
Original frequency of horn = f = 1200 Hz
Apparent frequency = f′ = 1140 Hz
Speed of sound = v = 340 m s⁻¹
Time = t = 50 s
Speed of source (i.e., train) = uₛ = ?
Distance covered by the train = S = ?
